name: Structural Chemistry
tagline: Crystal structures, bonding analysis, and molecular geometry.
seo_title: Structural Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Structural Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in crystallography, cryo-EM, stereochemistry and molecular structure.

definition.lead: Structural chemistry determines how atoms are arranged in space, in molecules and in crystals, and links that arrangement to properties.
definition.body: Shape decides almost everything: how a drug fits its target, why diamond is hard and graphite slippery, how DNA stores information. X-ray crystallography, NMR and electron microscopy are its eyes.

facts.label: Max von Laue shows that crystals diffract X-rays
the DNA double helix is built from X-ray diffraction data
structures stored in the Protein Data Bank

branches.name: X-ray crystallography
branches.summary: Diffraction patterns reveal where every atom sits in a crystal.
branches.example: Dorothy Hodgkin solved penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin.

branches.name: NMR structure determination
branches.summary: Structures of molecules in solution from nuclear spins.
branches.example: Proteins studied in conditions close to the cell.

branches.name: Cryo-electron microscopy
branches.example: Large protein machines that refuse to crystallize.

branches.name: Stereochemistry
branches.summary: The 3D arrangement of atoms and mirror-image molecules.
branches.example: One enantiomer of a drug can work while the other does not.

branches.name: Crystal engineering
branches.summary: Designing solids from molecular building blocks.
branches.example: Co-crystals that make drugs dissolve better.

branches.name: Conformational analysis
branches.summary: The shapes molecules take by rotating around single bonds.

branches.name: Coordination geometry
branches.summary: How ligands arrange themselves around a metal ion.

branches.name: Structural biology
branches.summary: The shapes of proteins and nucleic acids, and how shape gives function.
branches.example: AI now predicts protein structures from their sequence.

timeline.title: Mirror-image crystals
timeline.text: Louis Pasteur separates left- and right-handed crystals of a tartrate salt by hand.

timeline.title: Carbon is a tetrahedron
timeline.text: Van 't Hoff and Le Bel independently propose that carbon's bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron.
timeline.why: The start of 3D thinking in chemistry.

timeline.title: Coordination theory
timeline.text: Alfred Werner explains how ligands surround a central metal ion.
timeline.why: Founded coordination chemistry; Nobel Prize in 1913.

timeline.title: Crystals diffract X-rays
timeline.text: Max von Laue shows that a crystal acts as a diffraction grating for X-rays.
timeline.why: Atoms could now be located experimentally.

timeline.title: Bragg's law
timeline.text: William Henry and William Lawrence Bragg solve the first crystal structures, including table salt.

timeline.title: The double helix
timeline.text: Watson and Crick propose the structure of DNA, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.
timeline.why: Showed how genetic information is stored and copied.

timeline.title: The first protein structure
timeline.text: John Kendrew solves the 3D structure of myoglobin.
timeline.why: Proteins became objects with a visible shape.

timeline.title: The Protein Data Bank
timeline.text: A public archive for 3D structures of biological molecules is created.
timeline.why: Now one of the most used databases in science.

timeline.title: Cryo-EM
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Dubochet, Frank and Henderson for cryo-electron microscopy.
timeline.why: Structures of molecules that cannot be crystallized.

timeline.title: AI predicts protein structures
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to David Baker, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein design and structure prediction.
timeline.why: Structures that took years can now be predicted in minutes.

quiz.q: Bragg's law, nλ = 2d sin θ, links the X-ray wavelength to…
quiz.explain: Measuring the diffraction angles gives the distances d between layers of atoms.

quiz.q: Why are X-rays used to determine crystal structures?
options: Their wavelength is similar to the distances between atoms
They are visible, so the crystal can be photographed
They are cheap to produce in any laboratory
They melt crystals into a readable pattern
quiz.explain: Diffraction needs a wavelength comparable to the spacing, about 1 ångström.

options: Mirror-image crystals of a tartrate salt
Isotopes of uranium by their mass
The gases that make up air
quiz.explain: Their solutions rotated polarized light in opposite directions, revealing molecular handedness.

quiz.q: A chiral molecule is one that…
options: Cannot be superimposed on its mirror image

quiz.q: What is the most stable conformation of cyclohexane?
quiz.explain: In the chair every C–C bond is staggered and angles stay near the tetrahedral value.

quiz.q: What is the shape of SF₆?
quiz.explain: Six fluorines point to the corners of an octahedron around sulfur.

quiz.q: VSEPR theory predicts that a water molecule is…
quiz.explain: Two lone pairs push the two O–H bonds together, to about 104.5°.

quiz.q: In cryo-electron microscopy, molecules are imaged…
options: Frozen in a thin layer of glass-like ice
quiz.explain: Vitreous ice preserves the molecules in a near-native state.

quiz.q: Who solved the structures of penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin?
quiz.explain: She received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964.

quiz.q: What is the 'phase problem' in crystallography?
options: Diffraction records intensities but loses the phases of the waves
The phases of the moon disturb the data
quiz.explain: Both amplitude and phase are needed to rebuild the electron density.

quiz.q: The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry rewarded…
options: Protein structure prediction and protein design
Discovery and synthesis of quantum dots
quiz.explain: Batteries were 2019, click chemistry 2022 and quantum dots 2023.
